Ivo climbed down. “Eli’s opening the mural room tonight.”

“I know.”

“He asked whether you’d come.”

“I said I would.”

“He asked whether you’d actually come.”

Mara gave him a look.

“I told him you were elected and therefore obligated to appear at cultural events.”

“You told him I was his mother.”

“That too.”

They found Eli on the western wall, beneath a painted procession of people carrying buckets, pipes, books, blankets, seeds, and one enormous red kettle. The mural covered the outside of the old Directorate customs house. Where the wall had cracked, Eli had painted the cracks as rivers.

He stood on scaffolding, holding a brush in his teeth while he studied a section of faces.

At thirty-four, Eli had grown taller than Mara. He wore his hair cropped close and kept his harbor patch beneath his shirt, where it could not be read by passing machines. His hands were stained in six colors.

“You left out Minister Or,” Mara said.

Eli glanced down. “Did I?”

“There’s a small figure beneath the collapsed tower.”

“That’s not him.”

“Who is it?”

“Someone who may have carried a key.”

The figure’s face was turned away.

Eli climbed down. Children crowded around him, asking which parts were memories and which parts were invention. He answered each question seriously.

“The buckets are from witness accounts.”

“The blue fish are from a dream.”

“The woman with three eyes is not a historical person. She is a warning against believing paintings.”

Mara watched him with a tenderness that still frightened her. For years, she had treated his missing memories as a wound she was responsible for closing. Eli had taught her that memory could also be a room with no obligation to admit visitors.

He had drawn Sera only once.

She was standing at the edge of a crowd, her face left blank. Around her, children hummed four notes in differing keys. Some said the melody belonged to the old harbor engineers. Some said it was a lullaby from the drowned coast. Anja had found six versions and no first version.

On the mural, Eli had painted the notes as birds flying between districts.

“Do you remember her?” Mara asked quietly.

Eli followed her gaze.

“I remember remembering her,” he said.

The answer still hurt. It no longer demanded correction.

“I’m sorry,” Mara said.

“For what?”

“For all the times I told you what you remembered.”

“You were trying to give me something.”

“I was trying to give myself certainty.”

Eli leaned against the wall. “You can keep looking.”

“I do.”

“I know.”

In the evening, the children gathered in the archive courtyard for the lesson’s final exercise. Each was given a copy of a single event: the opening of Reservoir Six during the first night after the broadcast. One account came from a dockworker, one from a medic, one from a former security officer, and one from a child who had been carried through the crowd.

The accounts disagreed about who opened the gate.

They disagreed about whether the upper-district residents acted from generosity, fear, or the threat of dockworker retaliation.

They agreed that the water moved east.

“What do we write?” Jun asked.

Mara sat with them on the paving stones. “Write what each source says. Then write what can be confirmed. Then write what remains uncertain.”

“Which one is true?”

“Maybe all of them.”

“That’s impossible.”

“It is uncomfortable,” Mara said. “That is different.”

Jun chewed the end of his charcoal stick. “My grandmother says the assemblies are weak because they don’t know everything.”

“Your grandmother may be right about that.”

The children stared at her.

“We are weak in many ways,” Mara said. “We are slow. We argue. We fail to repair things before they break. Some people still hoard food. Some councils exclude people who speak badly or remember differently. We have made new rules that protect old prejudices. We are not good because we won.”

“What makes us good?” asked the winged-boat girl.

Mara looked through the open doors of the archive. Inside, lamps burned above the shelves. Every shelf held gaps where records were missing, sealed, or still being sought. On the highest wall, beneath the old painted warning, someone had added a line in white:

NO PERMANENT EMERGENCY.
NO PERMANENT LEADER.

“We are not good,” Mara said. “We are responsible.”

The girl considered this. “That sounds worse.”

“It is harder.”

After the children left, Mara entered the archive alone. Rainwater whispered through the gutters. Somewhere beyond the walls, a council had begun singing the founding song. Another district answered with the forbidden verses. Neither melody quite matched the other.

On her desk lay Sera’s final instruction, sealed in its protective sleeve. Mara had read it so many times that she could recite the worn sections by heart: separate it, do not shut it down; care first; never let one authority hold the story.

For years she had thought Sera’s legacy was hidden inside the machine, waiting for the right daughter to uncover it. Now the thought seemed childish, though not shameful. Sera had left instructions, not destiny. The rest had been made by dockworkers, frightened children, stubborn medics, tired teachers, people who opened reservoirs, people who admitted what they had done, people who stayed when leaving would have been easier.

Mara placed Oda Pell’s disputed testimony in its box.

Then she added her own correction.

Outside, the city bells rang again, irregular and overlapping. A warning sounded from the north tower, followed by a routine pressure notice from South Hook and a school announcement from Outer Nine. Three voices, none in command of the others.

Mara waited for someone to answer.

No single voice did.

The city answered itself: with hands at the pumps, with questions in the classrooms, with names copied carefully onto public walls, with food carried to strangers, with arguments kept visible until they could become decisions.

Nothing belonged to one voice.

Not the past. Not the harbor. Not the future.

Mara turned off the lamp and left the archive doors open.
